Appeals against administrative decisions

Description of the legislative solution

This legislative solution provides a right for a person to appeal against a decision that has been made under a statutory scheme, such as a decision of a public authority to grant or refuse a licence, issue a notice or make an order. An appeal is usually made to a court or tribunal, but sometimes to a Minister, department or other person who is independent of the original decision-maker. This legislative solution is concerned with appeals against administrative decisions, not with appeals against criminal convictions or against other judgments of the courts in criminal or civil proceedings.

A right of appeal may be an important means of ensuring that a process is fair and compatible with procedural obligations arising under the European Convention on Human Rights. Lawyers will be able to provide advice as to when an appeal procedure may be required. In general, an appeal is more likely to be needed if a decision has a significant effect on a person’s rights (e.g., their liberty, privacy, property or ability to carry on a business). Considerations of fairness and ECHR compatibility will also be relevant to the detailed questions in this legislative solution about the nature of the appeal.

Whether a right of appeal is required, and the nature of any appeal that is provided, will be affected by the adequacy of any other procedural safeguards in the decision-making process, because the question of fairness may be assessed by considering the process as a whole. An appeal may be particularly important if there is no chance for people to make representations before a decision is taken or confirmed.

A new right of appeal is likely to have impacts on the wider justice system, so it will be necessary to consider the impacts and associated costs and to consult accordingly.

A right to require the original decision-maker to review or reconsider its decision, or a system of alternative dispute resolution, may sometimes be provided instead of (or in addition to) a right of appeal. And in some cases the possibility of bringing a claim for judicial review of the original decision may be sufficient so that no provision for a right of appeal is necessary (although appeals may cover a wider range of grounds than can be raised in judicial review proceedings).

This legislative solution uses the following terms:

appellant – a person who is appealing against a decision;

appellate body – the tribunal, or other body or person, that receives and decides appeals.

Elements of the legislative solution

1. Which decisions can be appealed against?

1.1. Should there always be a right to appeal against decisions of the type in question, or should the right only arise if the decision has certain effects? For example, there might be a right to appeal against an order or notice only if it imposes particular types of restriction or obligation.

1.2. In the case of a decision that is made in response to an application, such as a decision whether to grant a licence, should the right of appeal attach only to certain types of decision that can be taken on the application? For example, should there be an appeal against a refusal of an application, but not against the granting of a licence? Should it be possible to appeal against the terms on which a licence is granted?

1.3. In cases involving applications, should the right of appeal depend on a decision being made, or should it also be possible to appeal against a failure to determine the application within a certain time?

2. Who can bring an appeal?

2.1. Should the right of appeal only be available to the person to whom the decision is addressed, such as an applicant whose application is refused or a person on whom a sanction is imposed?

2.2. Should other people who are directly or indirectly affected by a decision have a right of appeal? For example, if a decision has the effect of prohibiting an activity, should there be a right of appeal for anyone who has been carrying on that activity or intends to do so? What about people who are adversely affected by the fact that others can no longer carry on the activity?

2.3. Should other third parties have a right to appeal? For example, should a person who objects to the granting of a licence be able to appeal against the decision to grant it? Should such a right of appeal depend on the person having an interest that is affected by the granting of the licence, and if so, what kind of interest and what effect on it are required?

3. On what grounds can an appeal be brought?

3.1. Should there to be any limits on the grounds on which appeals can be brought? Legislation may simply confer a right to appeal against a decision without specifying any limitations, but in some cases the grounds on which appeals may be brought are specified. For example, the grounds for appealing against a notice requiring compliance with a statutory requirement might include:

that there has been no breach of the requirement in question;

that any breach that has occurred has not had detrimental effects;

that someone else was responsible for any breach that took place;

that the steps required by the notice, or the deadline for taking them, are impossible or unreasonable;

that the notice was not properly issued or served, or the notice or the procedure followed was defective in some other way.

3.2. In some cases, an appeal may only be brought on the ground that the decision was wrong as a matter of law, or on the grounds that can be raised on a claim for judicial review. For example, it may be appropriate to limit the grounds of appeal in this way if the original decision is made after factual evidence has been considered at a hearing or inquiry, or if it is a Ministerial decision in which policy considerations are likely to play a large part.

3.3. If the grounds of appeal are to be listed, care needs to be taken that potentially valid grounds are not inadvertently excluded. Note also that the grounds on which appeals may be brought will affect the procedures that are appropriate for dealing with appeals and the powers that the appellate body will need when it decides an appeal (see sections 6 and 8 below).

4. To whom must an appeal be made? And who is to determine the appeal?

4.1. Is there an existing tribunal, court or other body that is suitable to deal with the appeal (e.g., because it already deals with similar types of appeal or has relevant expertise)? If existing courts or tribunals are to be used, at what level in the court or tribunal system should appeals be considered (e.g., the county court or the High Court, or in Scotland the sheriff court or the Court of Session; the First-tier Tribunal or the Upper Tribunal)?

4.2. If appeals are to be made to Ministers [footnote 23] , should Ministers deal with appeals themselves, or should they be required to appoint another person to deal with them? Should the role of an appointed person be to decide the appeal or just to report to Ministers so that they can decide? Should Ministers have the power to remove and replace appointed persons, or to take over the handling of particular appeals from them? Should there be any limit on who they can appoint?

4.3. If no existing arrangements are suitable, should a new body or tribunal be created to deal with the appeals in question? Or should individuals or panels be appointed to deal with appeals on a case-by-case basis? If new arrangements are being created, what provision will be required for the establishment and administration of the new system? This might include provision about:

the appointment of members of the appellate body (including any chair or presiding member);

eligibility and qualifications for appointment to the appellate body;

different categories of member (e.g., legal or professional members and lay members);

duration and conditions of appointment;

removal and resignation of members;

remuneration and pensions of members;

responsibility for funding the appellate body and providing alternative support (including staff);

public accountability of the body and providing alternative support (including staff);

4.4. The decision about who should receive and decide appeals may be influenced by a number of factors, including:

who makes the original decisions that are appealed against;

the expected number of appeals and nature of the issues they will raise (including any evidence that will need to be considered);

whether using a particular appellate body will ensure fairness and ECHR compatibility;

cost, efficiency and convenience (which may count in favour of using an existing appellate body, where one exists, rather than establishing a new one);

relevant policies of the administration or legislature in question (e.g., policies that new appeals should be made to a particular tribunal).

5. Time limits and other requirements for bringing and responding to appeals

5.1. What rules should there be about how and when appeals can be brought, and about responding to appeals? If the appeal is to be made to an existing court or tribunal, there are likely to be general rules for proceedings in that court of tribunal that will apply by default to new proceedings that are added to its jurisdiction. In that case, consider whether there is already sufficient provision about bringing and responding to appeals in the existing rules, and whether any additional or different provision that is needed could be made under existing powers.

5.2. Should there be an automatic right of appeal, or should a person have to take other steps before exercising a right of appeal, such as requesting a review of the decision in question? Should an appellant require the permission of the appellate body to bring an appeal? A permission requirement might, for example, be used to determine whether a third party has a sufficient interest to appeal against a decision (see paragraph 2.3 above).

5.3. How much time should be allowed for bringing an appeal? Should it have to be brought within a particular period (e.g., a specified number of days) calculated by reference to when the decision is made or notice of it is given? Should an appeal have to be brought before something else has happened (e.g., before the decision has taken effect)?

5.4. Should the appellate body have the power to allow an appeal out of time, and should the power depend on particular conditions being met (such as the appellant showing a reasonable excuse for delay)?

5.5. Are there requirements relating to the way in which an appeal is to be initiated? Must a particular procedure or form be used, or must a notice of appeal contain particular information (e.g., the grounds on which the appeal is being brought)? Should any other information or documentation have to be provided when bringing an appeal (e.g., a copy of the original decision)? See also the giving notice legislative solution.

5.6. Should an appellant be required to pay a fee for bringing an appeal? If so, how will fees be set?

5.7. Should the original decision-maker be required to respond to the appeal? How much time should it be allowed for doing so? What must the response contain? Should the original decision-maker be required to provide any other documents or information?

5.8. If the intention is to set out the procedure for bringing an appeal or responding to it in subordinate legislation, what types of provision should it be possible to make about the procedure?

6. Procedures for dealing with appeals

6.1. What powers and procedures will the appellate body require for dealing with an appeal? If an existing appellate body is to deal with the appeal, are the powers and procedures of that body adequate or will they need amending to cater for the new rights of appeal?

6.2. What case management powers should the appellate body have?

6.3. Should the appellate body be given powers to make interim orders before the appeal is decided? The nature of any powers will depend on the subject-matter of the appeal, but could potentially include matters such as requiring undertakings or payments into court, or prohibiting steps that would undermine the proceedings.

6.4. Should an appellant be free to withdraw an appeal, or should this require the agreement of the appellate body?

6.5. Will anyone other than the appellant and the original decision-maker be able to take part in the appeal? Will a person who wishes to intervene in the appeal require the permission of the appellate body? How and when should an application to intervene be made?

6.6. How should appeals be determined? Should there be a hearing in person or virtually, or will the appellate body be able to make decisions on the basis of written submissions alone? Should a party to the appeal be able to insist on a hearing?

6.7. If an appeal is to be determined at a hearing, who should be able to appear at the hearing? May parties be legally represented at hearings? Should experts or other witnesses be allowed to give evidence?

6.8. If the appellate body is to consider evidence, what types of evidence will it need to consider? Will it need powers to require witnesses to give evidence or produce information or documents? Will oral evidence have to be given on oath (or by affirmation)? Should there be any limits on the types of witness or evidence that can be called? Should witnesses be entitled to allowances for attendance? Should failure to comply with a requirement to give evidence be a criminal offence? (See the criminal offences legislative solution.)

6.9. Should appeal proceedings take place in public? Will the appellate body need powers to share information with certain persons for the purposes of the appeal? Will it need to handle sensitive evidence or vulnerable witnesses? Does it need powers to exclude public access to any of the evidence it receives (e.g., on grounds relating to national security, commercial sensitivity or personal safety), or to facilitate the giving of evidence by vulnerable people? Should there be powers to order that parties are not named, or to restrict the reporting or broadcasting of proceedings?

6.10. Is provision needed about service of documents issued by the appellate body and sent by the parties (including electronic service of documents)? See the giving notice legislative solution.

6.11. If the intention is to set out the procedure for dealing with appeals in subordinate legislation, what types of provision should it be possible to make about the procedure?

7. Effect of a pending appeal on the original decision and on other legal proceedings

7.1. What status should the original decision have during the period in which an appeal could be brought or while an appeal is being considered?

7.2. Should the decision only take effect once the period for appealing has expired without an appeal being brought, or any appeal has been dismissed or withdrawn? Or should it be possible for the decision to take effect despite the fact that an appeal is pending or could still be brought (and then continue in effect unless the appellate body overturns or amends it)?

7.3. If the original decision can take effect despite the fact that an appeal is pending or could be brought, should the appellate body have the power to suspend the effect of the decision until the appeal has been determined or withdrawn? Should it be able to do so on its own initiative or only on the application of the appellant?

7.4. These questions need to be considered especially carefully in the case of a decision to revoke a licence or impose a prohibition if the consequence of the revocation or prohibition is that a business cannot continue in operation.

7.5. Should the decision-maker be able to withdraw or amend its decision while an appeal is ongoing? (Or in the case of an appeal against a failure to make a decision, should it be able to make a decision for the first time?) What effect should doing so have on the appeal proceedings?

7.6. If the subject matter of the appeal could be relevant to a matter in issue in a criminal prosecution or other legal proceedings, is provision needed to deal with the relationship between the appeal and those other proceedings? For example, should a criminal court be required to adjourn proceedings until the appeal has been determined?

8. Powers of appellate body when deciding appeal

8.1. What powers should the appellate body have when it decides the appeal? Should it only be able to confirm or set aside the original decision? Should it also be able to vary the original decision or correct errors in it? Should it be able to remit the matter to the original decision-maker for a fresh decision? Should it have the power to substitute its own decision, and if so, should it have to follow any requirements or procedures that apply to the original decision?

8.2. Should there be any limits on when the appellate body can exercise certain powers, or requirements for it to exercise those powers in particular circumstances? For example, it might have the power to set aside the original decision only if it is satisfied that there has been an error of law or fact, or it might be required to set the decision aside if it is satisfied that there has been such an error.

8.3. Should the appellate body determine the appeal only by reference to the circumstances at the time when the original decision was made, or should it be able to take account of a change in circumstances?

8.4. Should the appellate body have additional powers to give effect to a decision in favour of an appellant? Should it have the power to order the original decision-maker or anyone else to take action of any kind? If the effect of the original decision was not suspended pending the determination of the appeal, should the appellate body be able to award compensation to a person who has suffered loss as a result of the original decision? If so, should compensation carry interest?

8.5. Should the appellate body be able to award a party its costs of bringing or defending an appeal? Should any entitlement to costs depend on unreasonable conduct by the other party? An existing appellate body may already have powers to award costs.

8.6. Should the appellate body be required to publish or record the outcome in a particular way?

8.7. If the appeal is to an existing court or tribunal, some of these questions may already be addressed generally by the legislation that established it. And where there is provision for an appeal to a court under certain Northern Ireland legislation, section 22 of the Interpretation Act (Northern Ireland) 1954 makes general provision about the powers of the court in dealing with the appeal (including powers to remit cases and award costs).

9. Further appeals

9.1. Should a further appeal against the decision of the appellate body be possible, or should its decision be final?

9.2. If there is a further right of appeal, to whom will further appeals be made?

9.3. On what grounds will a further appeal be available? The possible grounds for bringing a second appeal are generally narrower than for the original appeal, and are often limited to points of law (as opposed to findings of fact or the exercise of discretion).

9.4. The answers to these questions may be governed by the decision about who deals with the original appeal; for example, if the original appeal is to the First-tier Tribunal, the default position is that a further appeal will lie to the Upper Tribunal on a point of law.

9.5. The considerations in sections 5 to 8 are also relevant to second appeals (although existing court or tribunal rules may already deal with some or all of those matters).

10. Effect of appeals on future exercise of powers

10.1. Should the fact that a decision has been successfully appealed prevent another decision of the same kind being taken in relation to the same circumstances? This may be particularly relevant to enforcement action and orders imposing requirements or prohibitions. An absence of restrictions on repeated attempts to impose the same measures may raise ECHR issues.

Fees and Charges

Description of legislative solution

This legislative solution allows for a person or body to charge fees in respect of a particular service or function that they perform.

The ability to charge fees — obviously — allows the fee-charger to raise funds. Importantly in many cases, it allows for the performance of the fee-charger’s functions to be funded by those on the receiving end of the functions, as opposed to out of general government expenditure. This legislative solution is therefore often useful in mitigating the cost to government of delivering a particular policy. For example, the costs associated with a licensing scheme might be covered wholly or partly by fees paid to the licensing authority by licensees, reducing or eliminating the cost to government of setting up and running the scheme.

“Fees” and “charges” are often used fairly interchangeably. “Fee” generally denotes an amount payable for a particular service. “Charge” may be more appropriate where there is a more indirect relationship between the amount payable and the underlying costs being funded. This guidance uses “fees” throughout for consistency.

It is important to discuss policy on fees and charges at an early stage with the relevant finance department or directorate. This is especially the case where the policy is likely to involve something more than the straightforward recovery of costs of particular services (e.g. where there might be variable fees or elements of cross-subsidy).

In the case of devolved legislation, legislative competence will of course need to be considered (and might pose difficulties where the policy goes beyond simple cost recovery, noting that taxation is not generally a devolved matter).

Related legislative solutions

A power to charge fees will often feature as a component of other legislative solutions. For instance:

A statutory corporation may be able to charge fees for carrying out its functions (see paragraph 14.5 of the legislative solution on statutory corporations).

Fees may well be payable under a licensing scheme (see paragraph 9 of the legislative solution on licensing).

A fee may be payable in respect of bringing an appeal (see paragraph 5.6 of the legislative solution on appeals against administrative decisions).

Another related solution is an industry levy, which might similarly be designed to allow a particular regulatory scheme to operate with less or no financial support from government. But generally it will be a charge in the nature of taxation rather than one associated with a particular service or function (see also the discussion above on “fees” versus “charges”).

Elements of the Solution

1. What is the fee charged for?

1. What are the services or functions whose performance may attract a fee?

2. Who charges the fee?

2.1. This might for instance be the Secretary of State, the Scottish Ministers, the Welsh Ministers or a Northern Ireland Department; or it might be a statutory corporation such as a regulator.

3. Who determines the fee?

1. Who is responsible for determining the amount of a fee?

2. Should that person be required to consult, or obtain the consent of, anyone else before charging the fee or determining its amount? For instance, if the fee-charger is a statutory corporation, should the government have input into the level of fees they charge? (See also paragraph 9.4 below on consultation in the context of regulations).

4. How is the amount of the fee determined?

4.1. What costs can the person who sets the fee take into account in setting the level of the fee?

4.2. The strong starting assumption is that a fee will allow for full recovery of the costs of the service to which it relates, but no more. Is there any desire to go beyond that? For instance:

4.2.1. Is the idea that fees should cover any enforcement costs associated with a particular regime? E.g. if a fee is payable in respect of an application for a licence, should the fee reflect the cost of enforcing breaches of licence conditions as well as the cost of processing the application?

4.2.2. Will there be any element of cross-subsidy — that is, any circumstances in which one category of fee-payer may be charged more than cost so that another may be charged under cost? An example might be a scheme under which companies are charged fees in proportion to their respective turnovers.

4.2.3. Is there a desire to be able to average out costs over a number of years? E.g., if fees in Year 1 are insufficient to meet costs, can an excess be charged in Year 2 to meet the shortfall?

4.3. Should fees be subject to a specific cap set out in legislation (e.g. a maximum fee of £100 for an application)?

4.4. Should the fee-charger be required to ensure that the fees it charges are sufficient to meet its costs?

4.5. Should fees be set in accordance with a formal scheme or methodology? (See also paragraph 9 below).

4.6. Should the fee-charger be able to charge a profit margin on fees? That may occasionally be wanted if a public body is providing services that might otherwise be provided by private sector bodies. It may in that case be appropriate to allow for fees to be imposed by reference to what the going commercial rate would be for the services provided.

5. Variation of fees

5.1. Is it envisioned that there should be a flat fee for a given service, or should the fee-charger be able to charge different fees in different cases? (This interacts with the comments on cross-subsidy in paragraph 4.2.2 above).

5.2. If there can be different fees in different cases, how much discretion should the fee-charger have? For instance:

5.2.1. Can they only vary the level of fees to reflect variation in the cost of the associated services?

5.2.2. Should they be able to take into account the wider circumstances in a given case, such as the nature of, or the financial position of, the fee- payer?

5.3. Should the fee-charger be able to waive or reduce the fee, either at their discretion or in particular circumstances? Or to provide for particular categories of person to pay a reduced fee or to be exempt from having to pay?

6. Timing of payment

6.1. Does the fee need to be paid within a particular period? Should the period be fixed or should the fee-charger be able to set it? Or is it enough for the fee- charger to withhold the service to which the fee relates until the fee is paid?

6.2. Should it be possible for a fee to be paid in instalments?

6.3. Should fees be chargeable on a periodic basis (e.g. an annual fee for being on a particular register, rather than a one-off registration fee)?

7. Use of fee income

7.1. Can the fee-charger hold on to fees they receive, or should they be required to pay fee income on to another person or to pay it into a Consolidated Fund?

7.2. Should the fee-charger be permitted, or required, to refund fees (in whole or in part) in certain circumstances (e.g. if a licence to which the fee relates is revoked)?

8.Enforcement

8.1. What should happen if a fee is not paid? Is it enough simply to say that the service in question will not be provided if the fee is not paid (e.g. the consequence of failing to pay a registration fee may simply be that one’s name will not be entered into the register)?

8.2. Alternatively is some additional provision needed to enforce the obligation to pay the fee (e.g. if a fee is charged in respect of services already provided)? For example:

8.2.1. Should unpaid fees attract interest?

8.2.2. Is a specific sanction appropriate for failing to pay a fee? For instance, if fees relate to a licensing regime, should there be an ability to revoke or suspend a licence if fees are unpaid?

8.2.3. Should failure to pay a fee be a criminal offence?

8.3. How is it envisioned that unpaid fees might be recovered? Would they be the subject of a civil claim in the courts, or is any other sort of recovery mechanism envisioned (for instance, a power to set off unpaid fees against amounts that might for other reasons be paid out to the fee-payer)?

9. Where will the fee amounts be specified?

9.1. Is it the intention to specify the amount of the fees in primary legislation or in regulations?

9.2. Or is it planned to specify the amount of the fees administratively? In that case, are the amounts to be determined by reference to factors, a formula or a methodology set out in regulations? Or is it possible to justify setting the amounts administratively without reference to anything set out in regulations?

9.3. If fees are specified administratively, how, when and where will they be published, and what exactly must be published (e.g. where there is a methodology underlying them this might commonly be subject to a publication requirement)? Should there be a requirement to publish fees (or any variation of fees) in advance of their coming into effect?

9.4. If regulations are involved, what scrutiny procedure in the relevant legislature should they be subject to, and should there be any requirement to consult a particular person before making the regulations?

10. Flexibility

10.1. How much flexibility should there be to depart from the fee arrangements that are put in place at the outset? Should the fee-charger have the ability to revise their methodology from time to time?

Providing Information

Description of legislative solution

This legislative solution involves requiring or authorising one person to provide information to another (or, to put it the other way round, enabling one person to obtain information from another).

Information may be provided in a very wide variety of circumstances and for a very wide range of purposes. For example, information may be provided to a particular person in confidence or may be published so that it is available to the general public; information may be provided for (and only for) a particular purpose or it may be provided with a view to achieving greater transparency, without restriction on its re-use; information may be provided to one person with a view to that person providing it to others, perhaps in the form of collated information, a report or a register.

Some of the elements below will be more relevant in some contexts than others.

A number of the elements below not only ask a question but also ask who should determine the answer, and how they should do so. That requires consideration of, among other things, whether it is appropriate for something (eg. the information to be provided or the persons to whom it is to be provided) to be specified or described in primary or secondary legislation (and subject to scrutiny by the legislature), or whether it is appropriate for that to be determined from time to time by a person by other means, eg. by a sectoral regulator.

In this solution, “information” generally includes “documents” (and see paragraph 2.4 below).

Related legislative solutions

Licensing: re-use of information may be authorised by means of licences

Powers of entry, inspection, search and seizure: powers to obtain information conferred on public bodies (eg. regulators) may take the form of powers to inspect, copy or seize information (eg. documents or information held on computers)

Criminal offences: duties to provide information, or restrictions on providing information, may be enforced by criminal offences

Civil sanctions: duties to provide information, or restrictions on providing information, may be enforced by civil sanctions

Giving notice: a notice may be used to require a person to provide information

Appeals against administrative decisions: a recipient of a notice may be given a right of appeal

Elements of the solution

1. Why does information need to be provided?

1.1. Why does information need to be provided? What cannot be done without it? What could be done better with it? How much better?

1.2. The reasons will affect the type of provision needed. Examples of reasons include–

to enable or assist public or private bodies to provide or improve services;

to enable a regulator to monitor, and enforce compliance with, a regulatory regime;

to enable the creation of, and access to, a register of persons or activities;

to provide transparency about a person’s or sector’s activities, whether activities of the person/sector providing the information or of others

2. Which information?

2.1. Which information is needed? Who should determine that (eg. the legislature, Ministers, someone else)? How should they do that?

2.2. Is the information needed likely to change over time? How quickly? How often?

2.3. Is it information that already exists, or information that will need to be generated by someone?

2.4. Are particular documents or types of document needed, not just information? (This is separate from the question about the form in which information is provided, see paragraph 6.1 below.)

2.5. Does the information consist of or include information that would be considered sensitive, such as information relating to individuals’ health or commercially sensitive information? If so, is the reason why that type of information is needed sufficiently strong to justify requiring or authorising it to be provided? (See also paragraph 3.9 below.)

3. Provided by?

3.1. Who should provide the information? Who is the best source of the information? Who should decide this (eg. the legislature, Ministers, someone else)? How should they decide?

3.2. Are the relevant persons likely to change over time? How quickly? How often?

3.3. Should there be a duty to provide information? Or just a power to do so?

3.4. Are there any existing duties or powers that already require or authorise the person to provide the information? If so, a new duty/power may not be needed. Consider both express duties/powers to provide information and general duties/powers that may impliedly include a duty/power to provide the information.

3.5. What currently prevents the person from providing the information? Consider possible barriers under the common law, in legislation or under contracts. There may be express exceptions from existing duties to provide information or express restrictions on existing powers to provide information (see paragraph 3.9below).Also consider other possible restrictions on providing the information, such as –

duties of confidentiality;

Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private and family life, home and correspondence);

data protection legislation (if the information concerned is or includes “personal data”, ie. information relating to an identified or identifiable living individual);

copyright, database rights and other intellectual property rights;

in the case of statutory bodies, the limits of their powers (see the Establishing a statutory corporation legislative solution).

3.6. Will the person required or authorised to provide the information already have the information? Or should the person be required or authorised to generate the information or obtain it from elsewhere?

3.7. Should there be a limit on how much effort the person must put into searching their records for the information or obtaining or generating it (eg. a limit referring to what is reasonable or to the costs involved)?

3.8. Is the information needed held by one person, or several persons? If it is held by several persons, how will it be brought together? By the person(s) providing the information, or by the recipient(s)?

3.9. Should there be exceptions from the duty to provide information? Or restrictions on the power to provide information? Should safeguards apply (eg. a requirement for the provider or recipient to have information security measures in place before the information is transferred)? Exceptions, restrictions and/or safeguards may be appropriate, for example–

for information that is commercially sensitive, or legally privileged, or whose disclosure could cause harm to individuals;

having regard to the circumstances in which the information was obtained, the intended recipient or the purposes for which the information must or may be provided.

3.10. Does the information need to be provided by a series of people along a chain? (For example, person A might need to provide information to person B who might then be required to publish it, with or without other information.) If so, consider each instance of the provision of information along the chain separately (and see paragraph 7 below).

4. Provided to?

4.1. Who should the information be provided to? Who should decide this (eg. the legislature, Ministers, someone else)? How should they decide? For example –

Should information be published so that it is available to the general public?

Or should information be provided to a particular category of people, eg. people involved in a particular sector or activity? If so, which people should be able to access the information and on what terms?

Alternatively, should information be provided just to a particular person, eg. a public body or a statutory regulator?

4.2. Are the people who need the information likely to change over time? How quickly? How often?

4.3. Does the information need to be provided to a series of people along a chain? If so, consider each instance of the provision of information along the chain separately. (See paragraph 3.10 above and paragraph 7 below.)

5. When is the information provided?

5.1. When should the duty or power to provide information arise? Should it be on-going? Or should it only arise at a particular time or times (eg. quarterly, every 5 years) or in particular circumstances?

5.2. Should the duty or power arise only if the information is requested, eg. by notice? If so –

Who can make a request? When? For what reasons?

Is provision needed about the form, content and timing of a request?

Should there be a deadline for responding to a request?

Should a person who receives a request be obliged to confirm whether they have the information? They may not have the information. Or, if they have the information, they may not be required or authorised to provide it due to an exemption or restriction (see paragraphs 3.5 and 3.9 above). It may be helpful for the person making the request to know which is the case.

5.3. Where information is provided, should there be a duty or power to provide updated information? If so, when?

6.How is the information provided?

6.1. Should the information be required to be provided in a particular form (eg. paper or electronic form) or by particular means? If it is to be published, where should it be published?

6.2. How prescriptive is it appropriate to be? Who should decide (eg. the legislature, Ministers, someone else)? How should they decide?

6.3. Is the appropriate form/means likely to change over time? How quickly? How often?

6.4. If the information is to be provided electronically, should use of particular systems or interfaces be required? Should a person be required to allow access to information held electronically?

6.5. Are there relevant standards or practices (either general or technical) that should be taken into account or complied with, eg. relevant sectoral standards or practices? Will new standards need to be established? If so, how and by whom?

6.6. Should requirements be imposed about the language or languages in which information is provided?

6.7. In considering these questions, think about the needs of different groups within society, eg. people who are unable or unwilling to access or provide information electronically or whose first language is not English.

6.8. In considering these questions, think about how you want, or expect, people to use the information and whether what is proposed will help them to do so. For example -

Does information need to be made available in a particular format, or through a particular interface, in order to be useful, eg. to make it possible, or easier, for information to be collated and compared?

Is there a need for people to be able to link related information, eg. different information relating to the same organisation or individual; the same information recorded at different times? Why is that necessary? What currently prevents that (see paragraphs 3.5 and 3.9 above)?

Consider how the link would be made, eg. should there be a requirement to allocate, and to publish, unique identifiers?

Consider whether linking sets of related information may change the nature of the information, eg. does the link make it easier to identify individuals?

7. What can or must a person who obtains information do with it?

7.1. How should a person who obtains the information be able, or be required, to use it? For example –

Should there be restrictions on how they use it? For example, should they only be allowed to use it for certain purposes?

Should they be required to retain the information for a period, or to dispose of it after a period?

Consider possible existing restrictions on how they can use information (see paragraph 3.5 above).

7.2. Should a person who obtains the information be able, or be required, to provide it to others (sometimes referred to as “onward disclosure” of information)? Or should that be prevented?

7.3. If onward disclosure should be allowed or required, consider the questions in paragraphs 3 to 6 above.

7.4. Will a person who obtains the information need to license the re-use of the information, ie. to make it available subject to terms and conditions? If so, is it appropriate to require the use of “open” licensing, ie. licences under which information may be used free of charge?

8. Enforcement

8.1. How should requirements to provide information (and any restrictions on doing so) be enforced? How should any restrictions on powers to provide information beenforced? How should requirements or restrictions relating to the use of information obtained be enforced?

8.2. Is there a need to protect information, eg. by providing that documents that are, or may be, required to be provided must not be altered or destroyed?

8.3. Who should enforce requirements and restrictions?

8.4. Should non-compliance with requirements or restrictions be enforceable by civil sanctions or by criminal offences?

8.5. If information is not provided, should the person who needs it have power to take action to obtain it, eg. powers to enter and search premises and to seize documents or information held on computers?

8.6. What should happen if someone under a duty to provide information intentionally provides incorrect or incomplete information? Or if they provide information without taking reasonable steps to check it is correct? Should there be civil sanctions or should that be a criminal offence?

Consider whether such behaviour would already constitute a criminal offence (see eg. existing fraud offences and other existing offences around making false statements and representations, mentioned in the Criminal offences legislative solution).

9. Registers

9.1. One way to provide access to information is for a person to bring it together in a register and make arrangements for access to the register.

9.2. Consider whether there are advantages to creating a register, or whether it is sufficient to require a person to publish the information.

9.3. If there is to be a register, who should maintain and manage it? Do they have any relevant general duties which might affect how they run the register, eg. duties to carry out functions with a view to achieving particular objectives?

9.4. Who should be able to access the register (eg. the public generally or only certain people)? On what terms? For a fee or free of charge? Should people be able to see the whole register or only to request particular information from it?

9.5. Should there be requirements about the form and content of the register, eg. how the information is presented, how it can be accessed electronically? How prescriptive is it appropriate to be?

9.6. Does provision need to be made to ensure that the register can be accessed both electronically and by people who are unable or unwilling to access it electronically?

9.7. Should there be restrictions on how information obtained from the register can be used? (See paragraph 7 above).

9.8. What provision is needed about verifying and updating information on the register, including about removing information from the register?

9.9. How should requirements and restrictions relating to the register, and information on the register, be enforced? (See paragraph 8 above).

9.10. In thinking about these questions, think about the different ways in which the information on the register may be used, not just for its primary purpose.

10.Consulting the Information Commissioner about proposals

The Information Commissioner must be consulted about legislative measures relating to the processing of “personal data”, ie. information relating to an identified or identifiable living individual [footnote 24].

These provide that service is effected where a letter is properly addressed, pre-paid and posted, and is treated as being served “at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post” (Interpretation Act 1978, section 7), or ‘on the day on which the letter containing the documents would arrive in the ordinary course of post’ (Legislation (Wales) Act 2019, section 14) ↩

A document sent by a registered post service or by recorded delivery is to be taken to have been received 48 hours after it is sent. ↩

Service of a document “may be effected by prepaying, registering and posting an envelope addressed to the person on whom the document is to be served at his usual or last known place of abode or business and containing such document; and, unless the contrary is proved, the document shall be deemed to have been served at the time at which such envelope would have been delivered in the ordinary course of post”. See also the Recorded Delivery Service Act (Northern Ireland) 1963 which means that section 24(1) of the 1954 Act also applies to documents sent by recorded delivery. ↩

Note that Part 1 of Schedule 8 to the Postal Services Act 2000 means that references to post, registered post, recorded delivery, first class post are not limited to the postal system of the Post Office. ↩

For Northern Ireland, see section 24(2)(e) of the Interpretation Act (Northern Ireland) 1954 which contains provision about service when the name or address of the intended recipient cannot be ascertained. ↩

Sections 13 and 14 of the Legislation (Wales) Act 2019 provide that service is effected if an electronic communication is properly addressed and is sent in an electronic form which is capable of being accessed and retained by the recipient. Service is deemed effective on the day the document is sent. Section 26 of the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 permits service by electronic communication where there is prior agreement. ↩
